target_claim: Running Dijkstra's algorithm (with re-insertion on distance decrease, as traced in the solution) on the explicitly defined family G_n (complete DAG on vertices v0..v_{n-1}, edge (vi,vj) for i<j with weight -2^i) performs at least 2^n - 1 Relax operations, i.e. R(n) >= 2^n - 1.
source_quote:
Let R(n) be the number of relaxations required for Gn. We prove by induc-
tion that R(n) ≥2n −1.
test_sketch: Implement G_n exactly as defined (lines 5-8: vertices v0..v_{n-1}, edges (vi,vj) for all i<j, weight w(vi,vj) = -2^i) and a lazy priority-queue Dijkstra that re-inserts a vertex whenever its tentative distance decreases (the variant the solution's own trace at lines 13-17 describes), with a counter incremented on every Relax call. Run for n = 1..12 and compare the counter to the claimed lower bound 2^n - 1. Because the weight -2^i depends only on the tail vertex i, extraction in min-distance order settles vertices after only polynomially many improvements: instrumented counts give relax(n) = n(n-1)/2 with standard tie-breaking (exactly one relaxation per edge) and at most ~O(n^3) growth (e.g. 231 at n=12) even under adversarial highest-index-first tie-breaking, versus the claimed 2^n - 1 = 4095 at n=12 and 255 at n=8. The counter falls short of the claimed exponential lower bound at every n >= 4, refuting R(n) >= 2^n - 1 by operation counts across input sizes. (The solution's induction also double-counts: it sums R(n-j) over the overlapping suffix subgraphs {vj,...,v_{n-1}}, which share edges.)
